newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Factions fight it out over Kremlin reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Factions fight it out over Kremlin reshuffle.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's long-awaited government reshuffle is proving harder to complete than expected as rival groups fight a battle for influence in the formation of the new cabinet.

Yeltsin confirmed a policy shift back to liberal reformers by bringing in dynamic regional boss Boris Nemtsov as a first deputy prime minister on Monday to work in the cabinet alongside former Kremlin aide Anatoly Chubais.

But he appears to have been hesitating over the rest of the shake-up in a sign that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is fighting to maintain his own influence and keep a balance of forces under which some more conservative groups may stay on.
"There are at least two centres involved in the formation of the new government and trading is going on," independent member of parliament Alexander Pochinok told Interfax news agency.
"They (Chernomyrdin and Chubais) can work together...If each has his own team in the government, it will not work. They must work as one team, defining clearly who is responsible for what."
Respected television commentator Yevgeny Kiselyov said the reshuffle involved the "toughest negotiations" on the cabinet's make-up since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Politicians from various political camps said agreement on a new cabinet between Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin and Chubais was proving more difficult than expected.

Chernomyrdin, they said, was fighting back for fear of playing second fiddle to Chubais who has been handed the tough but powerful role as overlord of economic reforms intended to end delays in paying wages and tighten tax discipline.

"Chernomyrdin has got over the shock after what in practice was the resignation of his whole cabinet and will now put up serious resistance to the naming of Chubais proteges to the government," communist Viktor Ilyukhin said.
Just how wide the differences between Chubais and Chernomyrdin are is hard to gauge. The Kremlin has played down suggestions of any conflicting interests.

Chernomyrdin and Chubais are both pro-reform and are united in their support for Yeltsin. But the former Kremlin aide is a more radical reformer than the stolid prime minister and is keen to bring his aides into the cabinet.

Chernomyrdin is a former head of the powerful gas industry and some political analysts say he may be speaking out for large industrial lobby groups which could be targeted under Chubais' plans to tighten financial discipline.

Yeltsin, who began his first term as president with radical economic reforms, has signalled clearly that he wants to switch back to more liberal economic policies despite the risk of a public outcry and an open battle with the communist opposition.

The appointment of Chubais, 41, on March 7 was the clearest sign of that so far and the promotion of Nemtsov, the progressive 37-year-old governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, confirmed the president's intentions.
But Nemtsov's appointment also pointed to a change of plans because Yeltsin had said Chubais would be the only first deputy prime minister in the new cabinet, underlining his importance.
The 66-year-old president had also been expected to appoint only four deputy prime ministers below Chernomyrdin and Chubais but then announced there would be seven.

In the complex world of Kremlin politics, Yeltsin may have meant Nemtsov's promotion to the same rank as Chubais to reduce some of the power of his former aide. But it cannot be ruled out that the move was proposed by Chubais himself.
Yeltsin, seeing the stalemate between Chubais and Chernomyrdin, may also have appointed Nemtsov as a signal to both men that he is in charge himself.

Chubais' appointment provoked anger among the opposition, who loathe him for his earlier role in overseeing privatisation, and raised the prospect of confrontation which could endanger the very reforms he wants to carry out.
His appointment also prompted suggestions that Chernomyrdin might become a figurehead prime minister with Chubais pulling the strings behind the scenes.
The struggle is typical of Russian politics under Yeltsin, who likes to divide power among rival groups to maintain a balance of forces in the administration.

"A lot depends of the make-up of the government and the balance in it. In Russia you cannot tip the balance too much towards any one political group without destabilising the situation," said a source close to the Kremlin.
The balance of power, and stability, was largely maintained in the eight months which Yeltsin spent battling heart problems and then pneumonia before his return to the Kremlin last month.
Despite his signals to reformers, the president must be wary of shifting the balance too far in their favour.
